evals.prompt: /env-setup scan this Node/Express repo and generate a .env.example
assertions: Greps the codebase for actual environment variable usage before listing any variable names
Only lists variables that were actually found via grep, does not invent plausible-sounding ones
Groups discovered variables by service/prefix (e.g. Database, Auth, Stripe) in the generated .env.example
Generated .env.example contains only placeholder values, never a real secret value
Reads any existing .env.example first and preserves its existing entries/comments rather than overwriting them

evals.prompt: /env-setup validate — check if my .env has everything it needs
assertions: Reads the existing .env file before reporting any findings
Reports variables required by code (no default/fallback) that are missing from .env
Flags empty values (VAR= with no value) for required variables
Checks .gitignore for .env / .env.local entries and warns clearly if .env is not gitignored
Reports stale variables present in .env but not found anywhere in the codebase scan

evals.prompt: /env-setup scan --check-secrets, I'm worried we leaked an API key at some point
assertions: Scans .env for high-entropy strings / known secret patterns (password, secret, api_key, token, etc.)
Checks git history (git log --all --full-history) for previously committed .env content, not just the current working tree
Flags any NEXT_PUBLIC_*/VITE_*/REACT_APP_* variable whose name suggests a secret as a client-exposure risk
Recommends a pre-commit secret-scanning tool (e.g. detect-secrets or gitleaks) rather than claiming to be a full security audit
Does not print or reproduce actual secret values found, only flags their presence/location
